title: context.Context: Done() Channel, Parent-Child Tree Cancellation

progressiveExplaining.eli5: A manager gives each worker a walkie-talkie on a shared channel. When the manager calls 'stop everything' (cancel), every worker on that channel hears it instantly and stops their task — and if a worker has sub-workers, the sub-workers hear it too (the signal flows down the tree). Workers can also set a deadline: 'if the order isn't done by 5pm, stop.' The walkie-talkie (the context) is passed from manager to worker to sub-worker, so a single 'stop' cascades through the whole team without anyone having to track everyone else.
progressiveExplaining.junior: context.Context carries cancellation, deadlines, and request-scoped values across API boundaries. Create with context.Background() (root), context.WithCancel(parent), context.WithTimeout(parent, d), context.WithDeadline(parent, t), context.WithValue(parent, key, val). Pass ctx as the FIRST parameter to functions that do work. Check cancellation: select { case <-ctx.Done(): ... } or ctx.Err(). Call the cancel function (defer cancel()) to release resources. Standard library APIs (http.Request.Context(), database/sql, net) honor context cancellation automatically.
progressiveExplaining.senior: Architecturally, a context is an immutable tree node: WithCancel/WithTimeout/WithDeadline create a CHILD context linked to its parent. When a parent is cancelled, the cancellation propagates to all children (and their children) via the Done() channel being closed. Each derived context holds a cancel function that unregisters it from the parent (avoiding leaks). ctx.Err() returns nil while active, context.Canceled after cancel, or context.DeadlineExceeded after the deadline. Values are a read-only key/value chain (WithValue); keys should be a private type to avoid collisions. The rules: never store contexts in structs, always pass them as arguments; never ignore the cancel function.
progressiveExplaining.underTheHood: The root context (Background/TODO) is an emptyCtx with a nil Done. Derived contexts use a cancelCtx struct: it has a done channel (created lazily), a mutex, children map, and err field. cancel() closes the done channel (once), sets err, and recursively cancels all registered children. timerCtx (WithDeadline/WithTimeout) wraps cancelCtx with a timer that triggers cancel when the deadline passes. valueCtx holds a key/value pair and forwards lookups to the parent (a linked chain). The Done() channel is the cancellation signal: select on it to react. The compiler/runtime has no magic — it's a plain data structure, which is why 'cancel leaks' happen when you forget to call the cancel function (the child stays registered on the parent).

codeComparison.title: Manual goroutine stop flag vs context cancellation
codeComparison.summary: A hand-rolled stop channel only handles one level and leaks on forget; context cascades cancellation through the whole tree and integrates with the standard library.

legacyOrBad.label: Manual stop channel
legacyOrBad.snippet: stop := make(chan struct{}) // ❌ OLD: one-off signal, no hierarchy

modernOrGood.label: Context cancellation tree
modernOrGood.snippet:
ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(context.Background()) // ✅ NEW
defer cancel()

interviewGotchas.question: How does cancellation propagate through the context tree, and why must you always call the cancel function?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: This tests the tree model — interviewers want the parent→child propagation and the resource-leak consequence of forgetting cancel(), which is a common production bug.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: Derived contexts (WithCancel/WithTimeout/WithDeadline) are child nodes: each registers itself in its parent's children map. When cancel() is called on a context, it closes that context's done channel (once, guarded by a mutex), sets the err, and recursively cancels every registered child — so the signal flows down the entire subtree. Because children unregister themselves from the parent when they are cancelled, forgetting to call cancel() leaves the child registered: the parent retains a reference to the child (and its resources — timers, goroutines) for as long as the parent lives. In a long-lived root context, un-cancelled children accumulate — the classic context leak. The rule 'defer cancel()' exists precisely to unregister and release immediately.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: The naive answer is 'calling cancel is optional if the work finishes'. The child stays registered on the parent until cancelled — a slow leak in long-lived processes. Another trap: using context.WithTimeout without storing the cancel (withCancel(ctx, ...) style misreads) — the timer also holds the child until it fires. Candidates who describe the children map and the unregister-on-cancel behavior show real understanding.

interviewGotchas.question: When should you use context.WithValue, and why is it discouraged for passing parameters?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: This tests the values mechanism and its design constraints — interviewers want the key-type guidance and the 'context is for request-scoped data, not parameters' rule.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: context.WithValue attaches a key/value pair to the context for REQUEST-SCOPED data that flows across API boundaries — e.g. a request ID, a tracing span, an authenticated user. The rules: the key must be a custom, unexported type (or a type you own) to prevent collisions with other packages; the value must be safe for concurrent use (contexts are shared across goroutines); and values should be few. It is discouraged as a general parameter-passing mechanism because it's opaque (no compile-time checking), hides dependencies, and makes functions harder to test — prefer explicit parameters for the data a function genuinely needs. The lookup is a chain walk (valueCtx forwards to the parent), so deep chains are slightly slower. context.WithValue never cancels; it's purely a value carrier.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: The naive answer is 'use context for any shared data'. It's for request-scoped metadata crossing boundaries, not business parameters — overuse hides dependencies and breaks readability. Another trap: using a string or a built-in type as the key — two packages could collide; the convention is an unexported type per package. Candidates who state the key-type rule and the scope guidance show real understanding.
